J Clin Oncol 1999; 17: 3835–49. CHRONIC LYMPHOCYTIC LEUKAEMIA. Chronic lym- phocytic leukaemia (CLL) typically occurs in people over 60 years of age, and accounts for about 30% of leukaemias in the West although it is rarer in the Far East. Stages of CLL are defined according to the Amer- ican Rai system or the European Binet system, with both having prognostic value.1-6 The clinical course is variable: low-risk patients (Rai stage O; Binet stage A) have a median survival of about 10 years, while high- risk patients (Rai stage III/IV; Binet stage C) have a me- dian survival of about 1.5 years; median survival in the intermediate stages is about 6 years.1,2 The mutational status of the immunoglobulin IGHV gene also affects prognosis; attempts to use surrogate markers of this sta- tus included CD38 and ZAP-70, and these have assisted in further risk stratification.6-9 In patients at low risk and those at intermediate risk with indolent disease cytotoxic chemotherapy is usually de- ferred until signs and symptoms of disease progression oc- cur.1,2,4-7 In these patient groups, trials of immediate versus deferred chemotherapy for early-stage CLL have shown no significant advantage, or disadvantage, for immediate chemotherapy in terms of 10-year survival.10 Patients with high-risk or progressive disease are usually treated with immediate chemotherapy. When therapy is required, it is essentially symptomatic and palliative. Continuous or intermittent chlorambucil has been most widely used, and is given for as long as the patient responds; response rates range from about 40 to 70%.2,3,7 Fludarabine is also used as initial therapy, and while response rates have been found to be higher than with chlorambucil,11 there appears to be no overall advan- tage in terms of survival.1,2,4,5,7,12 Compared with chlor- ambucil, the increased incidence of opportunistic infec- tions is a disadvantage of fludarabine treatment.4 The or- der in which alkylating agents and purine analogues are given is not thought important, provided patients who re- lapse on one treatment then receive the other.9 Although chlorambucil is often used with a cortico
